# Proof

**Claim:** Yes. The Taylor series of $f$ at every point of $\mathbb{R}$ uniquely determines $f$. In fact, the Taylor series at any *single* point already determines $f$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

---

**Proof.**

Let $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be analytic functions, and suppose that for every $x_1 \in \mathbb{R}$, the Taylor series of $f$ and $g$ centered at $x_1$ coincide. We show $f \equiv g$.

Define the set
$$S = \bigl\{x \in \mathbb{R} : f^{(n)}(x) = g^{(n)}(x) \text{ for all } n \ge 0\bigr\}.$$

Equivalently, $S$ is the set of points at which $f$ and $g$ have the same Taylor series. By hypothesis $S = \mathbb{R}$, but we will only need $S \neq \emptyset$.

**$S$ is nonempty.** Pick any $x_1 \in \mathbb{R}$; by hypothesis the Taylor series of $f$ and $g$ at $x_1$ agree, so $x_1 \in S$.

**$S$ is closed.** Each map $x \mapsto f^{(n)}(x) - g^{(n)}(x)$ is continuous (in fact analytic), so $S = \bigcap_{n \ge 0} \bigl(f^{(n)} - g^{(n)}\bigr)^{-1}(\{0\})$ is an intersection of closed sets.

**$S$ is open.** Let $x_0 \in S$. Since $f$ and $g$ are analytic at $x_0$, there exists $\rho > 0$ such that both Taylor series converge to their respective functions on $(x_0 - \rho, x_0 + \rho)$. Because $x_0 \in S$, all derivatives of $f$ and $g$ agree at $x_0$, so the two Taylor series are *identical* as power series. Hence
$$f(x) = g(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (x_0 - \rho, x_0 + \rho).$$
A real-analytic function that vanishes on an open interval vanishes identically there together with all its derivatives, so $f^{(n)}(x) = g^{(n)}(x)$ for all $x$ in this interval and all $n$. Thus $(x_0 - \rho, x_0 + \rho) \subseteq S$, proving $S$ is open.

**Conclusion.** $S$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is both open and closed. Since $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, $S = \mathbb{R}$. In particular $f(x) = g(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Therefore the collection of Taylor series (one centered at each point of $\mathbb{R}$) uniquely determines $f$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Remark.** The argument shows something stronger: the hypothesis "$S = \mathbb{R}$" was never used beyond the single fact that $S \neq \emptyset$. Thus the Taylor series of an analytic function at **one** point already determines the function on all of $\mathbb{R}$, via the connectedness argument above (analytic continuation along the real line). Knowing the Taylor series at *every* point is therefore far more information than necessary.

### PROOF COMPLETE
